summary.text: Lucas congruences pair the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\) to show that both sequences vanish modulo \(p\) at every \(p+r\) with \(0\le r<p\); at \(p-1\), the first value is \(1\), while divisibility of the central binomial factors kills every term except the midpoint in the second sum, giving \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\). Hence reversing the columns makes each Hankel matrix triangular with constant diagonal, and combining its diagonal product with the reversal sign \((-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\) yields the two claimed residues.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                 \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and perform all calculations below in the field \(\mathbb F_p\), unless otherwise stated. Put
\[
B(t)=\binom{2t}{t}.
\]
We will first establish the congruences for the sequence values that force the two Hankel matrices to become anti-triangular modulo \(p\).

We use the following elementary form of Lucas's congruence. If \(0\le b,d<p\), then
\[
\binom{ap+b}{cp+d}\equiv \binom ac\binom bd\pmod p.
\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, in \(\mathbb F_p[x]\), the binomial theorem and the freshman's dream give
\[
(1+x)^{ap+b}=((1+x)^p)^a(1+x)^b
\equiv (1+x^p)^a(1+x)^b.
\]
Since every exponent occurring in \((1+x)^b\) lies between \(0\) and \(b<p\), a term on the right has degree congruent to \(d\pmod p\) only when its exponent contributed by \((1+x)^b\) is exactly \(d\). Comparing the coefficient of \(x^{cp+d}\) proves (1). As usual, \(\binom bd=0\) when \(d>b\).

In particular, for \(0\le r,s<p\), (1) gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{s}\equiv \binom rs,
\qquad
\binom{p+r}{p+s}\equiv \binom rs.
\tag{2}
\]
We will also need two facts about central binomial coefficients.

First, if \(0\le u<p\) and \(p\le 2u\), then
\[
B(u)=\binom{2u}{u}\equiv0\pmod p.
\tag{3}
\]
For in that case
\[
2u=p+(2u-p),
\]
where \(0\le 2u-p<p\), while \(u<p\). Lucas's congruence gives
\[
\binom{2u}{u}\equiv \binom10\binom{2u-p}{u}=0,
\]
because \(2u-p<u\), the latter inequality being equivalent to \(u<p\).

Second, for every \(0\le u<p\),
\[
B(p+u)\equiv 2B(u)\pmod p.
\tag{4}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2u<p\), then
\[
2(p+u)=2p+2u,
\]
and Lucas gives
\[
\binom{2(p+u)}{p+u}
\equiv \binom21\binom{2u}{u}=2B(u).
\]
If instead \(p\le2u\), then the right side is zero by (3). The left side is also zero: writing
\[
2(p+u)=3p+(2u-p),\qquad p+u=p+u,
\]
Lucas's congruence contains the low-digit factor \(\binom{2u-p}{u}=0\). This proves (4) in both cases.

We next prove that, for every integer \(r\) with \(0\le r<p\),
\[
a(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p.
\tag{5}
\]
Split the defining sum at \(p\):
\[
a(p+r)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^4
       +\sum_{s=0}^{r}(-1)^{p+s}\binom{p+r}{p+s}^4.
\]
By the first congruence in (2), the terms in the first sum with \(k>r\) vanish, because \(\binom rk=0\). Thus that first sum may be truncated to \(0\le s\le r\). For such \(s\), both congruences in (2) show that the term with index \(s\) in the first sum and the term with index \(p+s\) in the second sum have the same fourth power \(\binom rs^4\). Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+s}=-(-1)^s.
\]
Consequently these two terms cancel for every \(s=0,\ldots,r\), proving (5).

There is an analogous cancellation for \(c\). Namely, for every \(0\le r<p\),
\[
c(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p.
\tag{6}
\]
Again split the sum into indices \(k<p\) and indices \(k=p+s\). In the first part, (2) makes the binomial factor \(\binom{p+r}{k}\) vanish when \(k>r\), so only \(k=s\), with \(0\le s\le r\), remain. Pair this term with the term indexed by \(p+s\). For the first term, (2) and (4) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^s\binom{p+r}{s}^2 B(s)B(p+r-s)\\
&\qquad\equiv (-1)^s\binom rs^2B(s)\,2B(r-s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
Here \(r-s<p\), so (4) applies to \(B(p+(r-s))\). For the term with index \(p+s\), we have \((p+r)-(p+s)=r-s\), and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^{p+s}\binom{p+r}{p+s}^2 B(p+s)B(r-s)\\
&\qquad\equiv -(-1)^s\binom rs^2\,2B(s)B(r-s),
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
again by (2), (4), and the oddness of \(p\). The expressions in (7) and (8) are negatives of one another. Pairing them for all \(s=0,\ldots,r\) proves (6).

We now evaluate the two values lying on the future anti-diagonal. Write
\[
p=2m+1,
\qquad m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
For every \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\pmod p.
\tag{9}
\]
One way to see this is to use
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}=\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}.
\]
Since \(k<p\), the denominator \(k!\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), while the numerator is congruent to
\((-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)=(-1)^k k!\). This proves (9).

It follows at once that
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k=1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, the fourth power of \((-1)^k\) is \(1\), and the alternating sum has the odd number \(p=2m+1\) of terms, so all adjacent pairs cancel and one \(1\) remains.

For \(c(p-1)\), almost every summand is zero modulo \(p\). Its summand at \(k\) is
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^2 B(k)B(p-1-k).
\tag{11}
\]
If \(k<m\), put \(u=p-1-k=2m-k\). Then \(u<p\), and
\[
2u=4m-2k\ge 2m+2=p+1>p,
\]
where the inequality uses \(k\le m-1\). Thus (3) gives \(B(p-1-k)=0\). If \(k>m\), then \(2k\ge2m+2>p\), so (3) gives \(B(k)=0\). Therefore only the middle index \(k=m\) survives.

At this middle index, \(p-1=2m\) and \(p-1-m=m\). By (9),
\[
\binom{p-1}{m}=\binom{2m}{m}=B(m)\equiv(-1)^m.
\]
Writing \(x=(-1)^m\), the surviving term (11) is
\[
x\cdot x^2\cdot x\cdot x=x^5=x,
\]
because \(x^4=1\). Consequently
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m.
\tag{12}
\]

We now turn to the determinants. We first record the elementary anti-triangular determinant evaluation that will be used for both matrices. Let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<n}\) be an \(n\times n\) matrix over a commutative ring, and suppose
\[
M_{i,n-1-j}=0\quad\text{whenever }j<i,
\tag{13}
\]
and all anti-diagonal entries \(M_{i,n-1-i}\) equal a common value \(d\). Reverse the order of the columns. The resulting matrix has entries
\[
M'_{ij}=M_{i,n-1-j}.
\]
Condition (13) says that \(M'\) is upper triangular, and its diagonal entries are all \(d\). Hence \(\det M'=d^n\). The reversal permutation has one inversion for every pair of distinct positions, hence \(n(n-1)/2\) inversions and sign
\[
(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}.
\]
Column reversal therefore yields
\[
\det M'=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\det M.
\]
Since this sign is its own inverse,
\[
\det M=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}d^n.
\tag{14}
\]

Consider first the \(p\times p\) matrix
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p},
\]
reduced modulo \(p\). After reversing its columns, its \((i,j)\)-entry is
\[
a(i+p-1-j).
\]
If \(j<i\), then
\[
i+p-1-j=p+(i-j-1),
\]
where \(0\le i-j-1\le p-2<p\). Thus (5) says this entry is zero. The reversed matrix is therefore upper triangular. On its diagonal, where \(j=i\), every entry is \(a(p-1)\), which is \(1\) by (10). Applying (14) gives
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\]
Since \(p=2m+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=pm=(2m+1)m\equiv m\pmod2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^m=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\tag{15}
\]

Finally consider
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
After column reversal, its \((i,j)\)-entry is \(c(i+p-1-j)\). For \(j<i\), the index again has the form
\[
p+(i-j-1),\qquad 0\le i-j-1<p,
\]
so (6) makes the entry zero modulo \(p\). Every diagonal entry is \(c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m\) by (12). Formula (14) now gives
\[
\det C\equiv (-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p.
\]
But \(p(p-1)/2=pm\), so both factors on the right equal \((-1)^{pm}\). Their product is
\[
(-1)^{pm}(-1)^{pm}=(-1)^{2pm}=1.
\tag{16}
\]

Equations (15) and (16) are precisely
\[
\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p
\]
and
\[
\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
This proves both asserted congruences for every odd prime \(p\).
